general.temas: Recurring stories include the pardon and medical treatment of blogger Lerchek, Russia’s exclusion from the World Junior Hockey Championship and the closure of the Estonia-Russia border. The return of Starship and Joe Biden’s memoirs also appear in several outlets. Only Meduza highlights the protest in Prague in support of public media independence.
general.motivo_crispacion: The war between Russia and Ukraine, the reported attacks and the drones headed toward Moscow reflect heightened tensions. The accusations against Russian intelligence in Estonia, the border closure and Russia’s exclusion from the World Junior Hockey Championship add international and institutional friction. The protest in Prague and Biden’s comments about Zelensky also reveal political confrontations. News about the economy, culture, health and advances in space exploration partly offsets that climate.

Kommersant.resumen:
- A closed-door United Russia seminar addresses party tasks, internal threats and digitalization.
- Russian GDP grew 1% year on year in the third quarter, exceeding the ministry’s forecast.
- SIBUR is considering challenging British sanctions, and the Defense Ministry explains a new mechanism for arms exports.
- SpaceX recovered a Starship spacecraft with its tower’s mechanical arms; the Bank of Russia sanctioned an auditing firm.
- The front page includes cultural and sports news and coverage of blogger Lerchek’s medical treatment.
Kommersant.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although some headlines use wordplay and emphatic expressions such as “the god of jumps.”
Kommersant.sesgo: The selection gives space to Russian politics and economics from a mainly institutional perspective, alongside cultural, scientific and sports news. No conclusive political bias is apparent in the available text.

Rossíiskaya Gazeta.resumen:
- Russia will be excluded from the World Junior Hockey Championship; the Kremlin comments on the decision and the Russian Olympic Committee is preparing a complaint against the international federation.
- Russian defenses destroyed 67 drones heading toward Moscow, according to the city’s mayor.
- Iran says a deal with the United States is currently impossible because some of its demands have not been met.
- Moscow will review Estonia’s announcement of the complete closure of its border with Russia; a Finnish politician comments on its possible consequences.
- The front page also reports on the parliamentary opposition in Nauru, the Finance Ministry’s position on a tax and local Moscow news.
Rossíiskaya Gazeta.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “our boys,” “enemy drones” and a call for “tough measures” introduce emotional identification and confrontation, although many of the headlines maintain an informative tone.
Rossíiskaya Gazeta.sesgo: The front page gives particular weight to the perspectives of Russian authorities and presents the sporting exclusion and drone attack through a Russia-centered lens. The texts provided contain few direct statements of the positions of the other parties involved.

Komsomólskaya Pravda.resumen:
- Celebrity news predominates: births, weddings, entertainment and the activities of several singers.
- The front page explains the CAR-T therapy that Lerchek will seek in China and mentions cancer vaccines in Russia.
- Two headlines present accounts of Boris Johnson’s remarks about Russian vodka; another addresses Biden’s criticism of Zelensky.
- SpaceX catches a Starship spacecraft with the arms of a tower, according to the front page.
- The front page covers eating separately as a couple and a healthy Russian diet.
Komsomólskaya Pravda.motivo_populismo: Insults and sensationalism abound, including calling Johnson a “drunk,” saying Biden “lashed out” at Zelensky and claiming that Starship will change space exploration “forever.”
Komsomólskaya Pravda.sesgo: The selection favors entertainment, private lives and personal conflicts, with attention-grabbing headlines. The stories about Johnson feature a mocking framing that favors Zakharova’s account.

Védomosti.resumen:
- The Russian stock market ended the week with gains of nearly 1% in its main indexes.
- Putin pardoned blogger Valeria Chekalina; one story reviews other presidential pardons.
- According to The Washington Post, Marco Rubio intervened to weaken the Nvidia chief’s influence over Trump.
- Russian telecom operators and banks agreed to identify calls from banks.
- The front page includes historical and business features, as well as technology and entertainment stories.
Védomosti.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “deal of the century,” “secret plans” and “losing everything twice” add drama and sensationalist appeal.
Védomosti.sesgo: The selection combines economic and political news with historical, business and entertainment features. Some headlines favor attention-grabbing stories of rivalry, intrigue and overcoming adversity, with no clear political bias apparent overall.

Meduza.resumen:
- Russia’s under-20 team is excluded from the World Junior Hockey Championship in Canada.
- Hundreds of thousands of people protest in Prague in support of public media independence.
- Estonia blames Russian intelligence for an attempted arson attack on a defense company and announces the closure of its border crossings with Russia.
- War coverage includes Ukrainian attacks in Russia and an appeal from Zelensky concerning Starshield.
- The front page covers allegations against a Russian actor, a cyberattack, an aviation failure in the US, sports, film and international affairs.
Meduza.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “there are a great many testimonies” and the disparaging quote about the complainants add intensity and drama.
Meduza.sesgo: The selection highlights the war, tensions between Russia and other countries, and allegations against a Russian public figure. The headlines combine factual information with some attention-grabbing quotes and wording.

opiniones.comunista:
Russian GDP grew 1% year on year in the third quarter, exceeding the Economy Ministry’s expectations. I do not confuse that figure with an improvement in the lives of working people: the decisive question is who receives the fruits of growth and who controls investment.

That is why I find it revealing that the Finance Ministry opposes extending the windfall profits tax to banks, microfinance institutions and gambling companies. It is not enough to celebrate aggregate figures while declining to demand more from sectors capable of making large profits. I support progressive taxation to fund health care, education and other universal public services.

But the class struggle requires going beyond taxes: collective ownership and democratic control of strategic sectors would make it possible to direct society’s wealth toward the needs of the majority, rather than private accumulation.
opiniones.anarquista:
The closed-door United Russia seminar, where Kremlin officials assigned tasks to lawmakers, illustrates what I reject about party politics: decisions come from above while society is relegated to the role of spectator. Organized obedience is not participation.

I am also troubled that the treatment of a seriously ill person depends on money from their friends. I welcome that solidarity, but it should not be a privilege available only to those with connections. I want care guaranteed through mutual aid networks, open and sustained by those who need them and those who work in them.

And I look with hope to those mobilizing in Prague for the independence of public media. Without free information and the ability to organize on our own, individual and collective freedom are at the mercy of those in power.
opiniones.liberal:
I believe the Russian Finance Ministry is right to oppose extending the windfall profits tax to banks and other sectors. Taxing a profit because it seems excessive introduces arbitrariness and weakens incentives to invest. I prefer low taxes and stable rules, along with a government that spends less and is held accountable.

Russian GDP’s year-on-year growth of 1% in the third quarter exceeded ministerial expectations, but a single figure does not prove that the economy enjoys enough freedom. Prosperity requires competition, legal certainty and room for people to start businesses and bear the consequences of their decisions. That is also why I am troubled that lawmakers receive guidance from above at a closed-door seminar: a responsible parliament must deliberate and hold those in power to account, not simply follow instructions.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I do not confuse sovereignty with slogans. In the face of the drone attack on Moscow reported by the authorities, the state’s first obligation is to protect its citizens and strengthen the country’s defenses. But security also requires strictly controlled borders and a migration policy decided by Russia, not by economic interests or outside pressure.

The exclusion of our junior hockey team in Canada shows the extent to which sport can be subject to political decisions. We must defend our young people through the available channels, without expecting international institutions to act out of generosity.

At the same time, the closed-door United Russia seminar reminds me that national unity cannot be reduced to instructions handed down from above. I want leaders who are accountable and defend the country’s families and traditions, not elites who confuse their interests with those of the nation.
opiniones.centro:
Russia’s growth of 1% in the third quarter exceeds some forecasts, but I would not confuse it with a guarantee of well-being. A healthy economy needs businesses capable of investing and competing, alongside public services and social protection that allow the fruits of growth to be shared. That is why, in response to the Finance Ministry’s rejection of an expanded windfall profits tax, I prefer a debate based on its real effects, not slogans.

I am also troubled that the tasks of United Russia lawmakers are discussed at a closed-door seminar with Kremlin officials. A parliament serves its citizens better when it deliberates in public and can exercise independent oversight. And in Prague, the mobilization for public media is a reminder of something essential: reforming their funding may be legitimate, but their independence must be protected through clear safeguards and broad consensus.
